title: {c[dem-133][value]:.0f} {c[dem-133][unit]} put 2023 US electricity sales high; {c[dem-134][value]:.0f} {c[dem-134][unit]} put commercial sales low
subtitle: Whether an outlook ran high or low depends on its target. Each row compares one target year on one boundary. A diamond is a projection, a circle is what came after, and the bar between them is the difference. The two EIA rulers do not start at zero, so errors of a few percent stay visible.
text: Only the LBNL ruler counts data centers, and it holds one pair, read from charts: {c[dem-039][value]:.0f} TWh projected for 2020, about {c[dem-103][value]:.0f} estimated later. That is a fact about one report, not a record of data center forecasts.
The EIA rulers and the utility plans count whole sales classes. Rows show every second EIA edition; the counts cover them all. For 2019, {c[dem-132][value]:.0f} {c[dem-132][unit]} ran high.

reading_for.Projected total sales: EIA's {tag} outlook, published {label}, projected {proj} {unit} of US electricity sales for {year}, all customers and not data centers alone. The realized value is {real} {unit}. Realized minus projection is {diff} {unit}, or {error} of the realized value, so this projection ran {ran}.
reading_for.Projected commercial sales: EIA's {tag} outlook, published {label}, projected {proj} {unit} of US commercial-sector electricity sales for {year}, a class that includes data centers and is not a data center series. The realized value is {real} {unit}. Realized minus projection is {diff} {unit}, or {error} of the realized value, so this projection ran {ran}.
reading_for.Projection, 2016 report: LBNL's 2016 report projected {proj} {unit} for {year}. Its {label} later put {year} at about {real} {unit}. That estimate minus the projection is {diff} {unit}, or {error} of the estimate, on one scope and two methods. One pair is a fact about one report, not a record of data center forecasts.
reading_for.2014 base, 2016 report: Context, not part of the error: LBNL's 2016 report put 2014 at {proj} {unit}, and its 2024 Report restates 2014 at about {real} {unit}. Because the base moved, growth compares more cleanly: {c[dem-106][text]} percent projected for 2014 to 2020, against about {c[dem-107][text]} percent estimated. Limit: {c[dem-107][limit]}
reading_for.Base plan forecast: {label}'s first plan in the study forecast growth of {proj} {unit} to 2014, with its low and high forecasts in parentheses. Observed growth was {real} {unit}, below even the low forecast. Observed minus base forecast is {diff} percentage points, so this plan ran {ran}. No percent error, because observed growth near zero makes that ratio meaningless.
reading_for.Base plan forecast, Montana: {label}'s first plan in the study forecast growth of {proj} {unit} to 2014, with its low and high forecasts in parentheses. Observed growth was {real} {unit}, inside that range. Observed minus base forecast is {diff} percentage points, so this plan ran {ran}. No percent error, because observed growth near zero makes that ratio meaningless. The study does not group this Montana utility with the Pacific Northwest.

details: A projection is a scenario under stated assumptions, not a prediction: EIA's Reference case holds current laws fixed.
EIA rulers: EIA revises history after each edition's cutoff, so part of an older edition's gap is a later history revision and not a model error.

EIA rulers: EIA says the commercial sector includes data centers, but neither series is a data center series. How a utility classes a given data center, and why commercial sales beat most editions, were not checked, so no difference here is attributed to data centers.

LBNL ruler: both reports count servers, storage, network equipment, and infrastructure in US data centers, and LBNL plots the two on one axis in its 2024 Report. The methods differ, and whether the 2016 report counted cryptocurrency mining was not checked.

Utility plans: growth rates run from the first forecast year of each utility's first plan in the study to 2014 (the paper does not state that year; its Table 1 gives only the plan year), so the periods differ. These are plan forecasts, not outlooks, and none is a data center series. The observed rows are the utilities' actual loads, which embed the realized effects of their own energy-efficiency and demand-response programs.
